item.title: Gender Stereotypes Make Women Invisible: The Presence of Female Scientists in the Media
item.description: arXiv:2610.28640v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Interest in the situation of women scientists has increased in recent years. Scientific institutions and governmental authorities have launched initiatives to promote science as a vocation among women. Within this context, the effort made by the media in disseminating role models is of vital importance. The aim of this research is to analyse the presence of women scientists in the media, and to conduct an appraisal of the status granted to them and the image conveyed about them. To this end, we analysed the content published on the websites of the regional newspapers Berria, Gara, El Correo and Diario de Navarra between 2014 and 2019 citing women scientists and researchers (N = 2362). The results indicate that presence is greater in quantitative terms, as is the prominence given to them in headlines. However, the disciplines in which they practise and the stereotypes which are conveyed shape their image, which in the case of STEM areas emphasise their role as carers and their singularity in the scientific field.
item.dc:creator: Maider Eizmendi-Iraola, Sim\'on Pe\~na-Fern\'andez

item.title: Evolution of article processing charges in medicine: disciplinary position, access gaps and future prospects
item.description: arXiv:2610.28643v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Medicine occupies a singular position in the open access economy: It is the field with the highest number of OA journals with APCs in DOAJ, the second largest by global APC expenditure with high rates of APC adoption among researchers in the Global South. This article analyses APC trajectories in medicine from a comparative disciplinary perspective, drawing together evidence from multiple studies to position medicine in relation to other scientific fields over the period 2009-2023. It documents price gaps between medical and biomedical subcategories, the particularly acute affordability challenges associated with publishing in global health journals and the structural asymmetry between the public urgency of medical knowledge and the cost of its dissemination. The article concludes with a reflection on alternative models and the conditions required for an equitable and sustainable open access transition in medicine.
item.dc:creator: Prieto-Guti\'errez, J. J., Bl\'azquez-Ochando, M., Ovalle-Perandones, M. A

item.title: MultiphaseHUB for Evidence-Grounded Metadata Curation and Task-Aware Compression of Multiphase Data
item.description: arXiv:2610.28644v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Multiphase transport experiments and simulations generate high-dimensional data whose scientific value depends on the physical conditions, sensing configuration, calibration, synchronization, uncertainty, and provenance accompanying the raw signals. These data are difficult to reuse when experimental context is scattered across publications and repositories, while large measurement volumes increase the cost of transfer and analysis. In this work, we introduce MultiphaseHUB as a community infrastructure and an integrated framework for organizing, discovering, and reusing multiphase transport data. The infrastructure connects externally hosted datasets with modality-specific metadata, publications, analysis tools, derived features, source repository links, and boundaries for reuse. Within this framework, we develop two complementary components: literature analysis and data curation, comprising Large Language Model (LLM)-assisted metadata extraction and an agentic literature-analyzer for quantitative values from figures; and modality-specific scientific data compression guided by the quantities of interest needed for downstream analysis. These components address the effort required to interpret heterogeneous sources and the cost of accessing useful information from high-dimensional measurements. Public multiphase datasets provide seed resources for illustrating the framework and its workflows. Building on these components, we outline a research roadmap encompassing cross-facility harmonization, multimodal alignment, task-aware retrieval and dataset valuation, and conditional reconstruction of missing modalities. MultiphaseHUB provides a foundation for connecting distributed data resources to physically meaningful comparison and cross-study scientific discovery.
item.dc:creator: Yingyan Zeng, J. P. Panda, Avranshu Mahanty, Han Hu, Depeng Xu, Ying Sun

item.title: Peer review should constrain evaluative authority
item.description: arXiv:2610.28646v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Our position shifts the target of peer-review reform from reducing uncertainty through evaluator improvement or judgment aggregation to constraining evaluative authority under persistent uncertainty. Scientific peer review aims to assure research quality but also allocates scarce academic opportunities, such as publication in high-impact venues. However, the review system is under growing pressure as submissions increase while reviewer capacity, expertise, scrutiny, and incentives cannot scale accordingly. As peer review operates under persistent evaluative uncertainty, evaluator improvement and judgment aggregation remain structurally limited. We therefore propose authority-constrained peer review: before a consequential judgment is released as decision-relevant, it should withstand structured scrutiny through critique-authority decoupling, independent secondary evaluation, contestability and reversibility, and accountability for unsupported influence. Our aim is to prevent weakly supported judgments from entering final deliberation with the same authority as judgments that have withstood structured scrutiny, while creating incentives for reviewers to justify consequential claims more carefully. For large-scale computer-science conferences, this position offers an institutional response to uneven review quality and reviewer-assignment dependence; more broadly, it provides a governance principle for any domain where uncertain expert judgments allocate scarce academic opportunities.
item.dc:creator: Hanrui Wang, Timo Spinde, Isabella Habereder, Chun-Shien Lu, Isao Echizen

item.title: An Open-Source Data Infrastructure for Alloy Synthesis Research: Stage 1 --- Composition Screening and Literature Cross-Referencing
item.description: arXiv:2610.28647v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Experimental materials-science labs routinely accumulate synthesis and characterization data across spreadsheets, instrument export files, and ad-hoc folders, with no durable link between a sample's recipe, its measured properties, and whether a similar composition has been reported elsewhere. We present Stage 1 of an open-source data infrastructure closing this loop for a single working alloy-synthesis lab: a relational schema for composition and synthesis records, a strict composition/mass calculator, three empirical alloy-design screening metrics (VEC, atomic-size mismatch, mixing enthalpy) plus a melt/boil-point synthesis-feasibility check, an automated cross-referencing layer against three public materials databases (Materials Project, OQMD, Alexandria) with deduplication and adjustable relevance filtering, and a desktop GUI unifying the workflow behind a single "new entry" action. Built and used by a practicing researcher rather than a software team, we report it as a systems/methodology contribution - the architecture, the concrete engineering failures encountered while building it, and how each was diagnosed and fixed - rather than new materials-science results. We argue the specific defects found - a parser ambiguity that produced silent wrong answers, a partial code edit that broke a dependency chain invisibly, a database-metadata bug traceable to an un-cast numeric type, and a credential-hygiene gap that .gitignore alone did not close - generalize to any small scientific-software project built by a domain expert without formal software-engineering training. Both the system and the lessons from building it are reported here; two follow-on papers cover the validated characterization pipelines (Stage 2) and the retrieval-augmented synthesis advisor and CALPHAD thermodynamics module (Stage 3) built on this foundation.
item.dc:creator: Iliya Angelov Radulov

item.title: Building Knowledge Graphs for Theses: A Survey
item.description: arXiv:2610.28648v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Academic theses are a valuable source of scientific knowledge, yet their semantic exploitation remains limited. While Scholarly Knowledge Graphs have significantly advanced the representation of scientific publications, knowledge graph construction for academic theses has received comparatively limited attention. This paper provides a systematic review of existing approaches and analyzes their potential application for the thesis domain. We analyzed 46 peer-reviewed studies published between 2021 and 2025, and organised existing approaches into a structured classification of techniques, models, and tools. The review reveals a methodological evolution from natural language processing techniques for entity and relation extraction to ontology engineering, Semantic Web technologies, and AI-driven enrichment through knowledge graph embeddings, Linked Open Data, and Large Language Models. The findings provide a consolidated view of the current state of the art and identify methodological foundations and future research directions for building knowledge graphs for the thesis domain.
item.dc:creator: Donia Ruelas, Elmer Coyla, Miguel Aceituno, Elwin Huaman

item.title: Zero-Cost Detection of Fabricated Citations: A Staged Heuristic Approach for Computing Dissertation Assessment
item.description: arXiv:2610.28649v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Generative AI's growing role in academic writing has driven a rise in fabricated references across dissertations and student reports. We present the Fabrication Severity Stack (FSS), a three-tiered framework classifying citation fabrications by detection complexity - from non-existent references to subtle content misattribution. Building on the FSS, we propose a staged heuristic verification workflow, executable through mainstream LLM interfaces. We argue that this framework offers computer science educators/examiners a practical, zero-cost basis for embedding reference verification into the assessment of dissertation and students' reports. In a pilot study on 100 citations (20% seeded with Level 1 and Level 2 fabrications), the proposed heuristic workflow enabled mainstream LLM interfaces to correctly flag 9-10 of 10 non-existent references and partially detect metadata corruption. These preliminary results suggest that freely accessible, general-purpose LLMs can achieve high recall on citation verification without reliance on proprietary detection tools.
item.dc:creator: Hazrat Ali, Mohamed Elawady

item.title: The CIDOC CRM Periodic Table: Documentation You Can Test to Support the Adoption of Scientific Research Ontologies for the Humanities
item.description: arXiv:2610.28650v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The CIDOC CRM family is not only a schema for museum collections. Its extensions formalise the apparatus through which research knowledge is produced and justified: CRMsci models scientific observation and measurement, CRMdig the provenance of digital processes, CRMinf inference and belief. Together they constitute a schema for research data, and the obstacle to their adoption is documentary rather than theoretical: four normative documents, four code conventions, and eighty-nine typed links crossing document boundaries. This paper presents the CIDOC CRM Periodic Table, a single-page browser rendering 131 classes and 480 property entries from CIDOC CRM 7.1.3, CRMsci 3.2, CRMdig 5.0 and CRMinf 1.2.1 as one navigable surface, with two inference facilities: a one-step triple builder admitting only the class-property combinations licensed by declared domains, ranges and the subclass closure, and a multi-step path finder enumerating property chains between two classes. Because all loaded models are merged into one code-keyed dictionary before the hierarchy closures are computed, both resolve chains that cross model boundaries; we document the addition of CRMsci and the three cross-model tests it made possible, and report preliminary uptake signals from 56 months of analytics, with the reading they support.
item.dc:creator: Remo Grillo

item.title: The Scientific Research Taste Benchmark (SciTaste-Bench): A Multi-Disciplinary Benchmark for Assessing Large Language Models' Judgment of Research Taste in Scientific Papers
item.description: arXiv:2610.28653v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Whether large language models can assess the innovativeness of academic publications matters for literature reviews, research funding screening, and academic recommendations. We introduce the Scientific Research Taste Benchmark (SciTaste), a gold-standard benchmark covering six disciplines: physics, mathematics, chemistry, biology, medicine, and finance. SciTaste measures research taste, that is, the ability to judge a paper's scientific value and potential, of which innovativeness is one of seven dimensions. It integrates metadata from NASA ADS, OpenAlex, and arXiv, aligns papers to field-specific classification systems, and scores each paper with the seven-dimensional Academic Taste Index. Dimension weights come from a bi-objective machine-learning approach (five regressors, including random forests) and are shared across all six disciplines. The benchmark includes 300 selected papers (50 per discipline) and a backup pool of 5,700 papers (950 per field) covering 1996-2023. SciTaste supports four evaluation modes: pure_qa, native_search, our structured tool-calling agent DiM (9 bibliometric tools in ADS/OpenAlex), and dimagent_v3_native. Outputs are evaluated by two complementary schemes: correlation with dimension-level accuracy, and WAPE relative error. Across ten state-of-the-art LLMs, tool-based structured evaluation generally outperformed toolless and raw web search modes, though gains were model-dependent. Physics is easiest; chemistry, biology, and medicine remain more challenging. SciTaste supplies the value-judgment substrate auto-research systems need to screen, rank, and prioritize candidate ideas. Dataset, harness, and scoring code are available on Hugging Face at https://huggingface.co/datasets/skylenage/SciTaste-benchmark.
item.dc:creator: Xinyi Gao, Xiaogang Li, Jialu Nie, Yuting Fu, Jingye Xu, Xinyan Liu, Muxi Zheng, Xiao Zhou, Wenbo Li, Xuan Ren, Hu Wei, Bing Zhao

item.title: What Git Does Not Record: Provenance Legibility in Two AI-Assisted Research Repositories
item.description: arXiv:2610.28655v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Publishers and funders increasingly ask authors to disclose how AI tools contributed to a piece of research. In computational work the repository is where an author or an auditor would look for the answer, and we ask what it can actually supply. We audit two single-investigator repositories by the same author in the same field, each carrying a different class of agent residue: a prescriptive trace of standing rule files and a narrative trace of a running agent scratchpad, in repositories of 466 and 103 commits. The two are legible in opposite ways. 85.6% of the lines ever committed to the prescriptive trace are visible at the current revision, and a standing rule states a conclusion and discards the episode behind it; the narrative trace records episodes and shows 21.8%. Counted by revision the gap is far smaller: 15 of the prescriptive trace's 41 revisions leave no visible line, against 18 of the narrative trace's 41. The Co-Authored-By trailer, the field an automated audit reads, is one of three AI trailer keys Project A carries and covers 66 of the 121 commits carrying any. In Project B it has low sensitivity against an explicit within-repository proxy: 39 commits revise a file maintained to hold an agent's working notes and 1 (2.6%) carries the trailer. Project A's repository-level rate is unstable in time too, stepping from 2.7% to 17.7% across a boundary we did not specify in advance. Repository channels disagree, and neither rate can be read as an involvement rate; we do not isolate the cause, and say so. We give a field-by-field account of which provenance claims such traces support, which they cannot, and which they answer confidently and wrongly, construct an auditable evidence ledger, and derive the requirements this places on any system meant to record research provenance as it happens.
item.dc:creator: Koutian Wu, Zesen Huang, Hejia Geng

item.title: FutureLens: Longitudinal Topic Patterns in Scholarly Text and Future-Work References
item.description: arXiv:2610.28656v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Future-work statements offer a record of the questions researchers choose to leave open. Using them to describe a field, however, requires separating thematic change from changes in document coverage, topic assignment, and scholarly writing. FutureLens examines these measurement issues in a recovered snapshot of 5,655 ACL papers published during 2012--2022, including 4,005 with supplied future-work reference text. We compare non-negative matrix factorization (NMF) and latent Dirichlet allocation (LDA), aggregate topic presence at the paper level, and examine normalized prevalence, exploratory trend statistics, assignment stability, and agreement between input-derived text and references. Across available seeds, NMF has higher mean normalized pointwise mutual information (0.1387 versus 0.1280) and higher pairwise assignment stability, while LDA has greater keyword diversity (0.8900 versus 0.7750). Seed-zero results show increasing prevalence of broad model-training and question-related vocabulary, alongside substantial citation and document-structure content. Mean input/reference topic-set overlap is 0.5191 for NMF and 0.4924 for LDA; temporal rank agreement varies widely and does not imply agreement in prevalence levels. These findings support a descriptive account of the available corpus, with explicit qualifications for missing references, incomplete runs, and unverified reference provenance. The contribution is an empirical measurement study of longitudinal scholarly signals, not a new topic-modeling algorithm or a forecasting system.
item.dc:creator: Ibrahim Al Azher, Hamed Alhoori

item.title: CompLit: Scientific Literature Search Benchmarks Must Cover Implicit, Cumulative, and Unmet Needs
item.description: arXiv:2610.28658v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: How much can we trust an agent to find the paper we need? As researchers, we search the literature from what we have read toward what we have not. We thus describe what we want in our own terms, which a paper may show only implicitly; our requirements grow as we read; and what we seek may lie in an empty region no paper yet covers. We introduce CompLit, a literature search benchmark spanning all eight arXiv domains, with one diagnostic setting for each of these needs. The strongest agents, Codex (GPT-5.6-Sol) and Claude Code (Opus 4.8), answer 86-87% of Standard queries, yet fall to 66-68% when requirements are implicit (implicit), lose another 6 and 15pp, respectively, as they accumulate (cumulative), and abstain on at most 53% of the queries no paper satisfies (unmet). No agent leads in every domain, and all are less accurate on papers from before 2019 or after 2023. Tracing their search, we find that agents often reach the right paper, or the closest one, yet misjudge it. Doing well on CompLit is a step toward agents that we can trust to find the paper we need, or to tell us that none exists.
item.dc:creator: Dayoon Ko, Jihyuk Kim, Soyeong Jeong, Young-jun Lee, Dahyun Lee, Juyeon Kim, Gunhee Kim, Moontae Lee, Kyungjae Lee

item.title: Beyond source attribution: Address authorship and comparability decisions in an LLM-built scholarly knowledge graph
item.description: arXiv:2610.28663v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: A knowledge graph needs a stable address for its evidence even where the literature offers competing classifications and agrees on none. Yet an address chosen for retrieval readily passes for the only classification available. This happens whenever records gathered under one name concern units that differ in boundaries, rank, or the criteria by which they are described or counted. In Sinitic dialectology the same localities recur in schemes whose units differ in membership and rank, and a unit may change its affiliation when the evidence for its diagnosis changes. Two tone counts, each quoted faithfully, may still count different things. The taxonomy of an entire field thus comes to rest on the unstable frame of a literature that contradicts itself. Neither verifying a quotation nor searching for conflicting values detects these differences. I distinguish the working address that gathers candidate evidence, the category that the source defines and the decision that admits a passage to a particular comparison, and argue that such decisions, together with the dependence among records, belong to the provenance of a comparison. On four re-runnable cases, the accompanying PaRAGraph Casebook shows where such differences arise among claims extracted by a language model and verified before entering the graph. The platform now stores the corresponding decisions as objects for one dimension of comparability, the address of a record: the placement of a locality in each source's scheme, the decision that a name in a given publication denotes a unit rather than a place, and the origin of every address. The working taxonomy can then be revised as new sources yield new claims, while the path from each comparison to its evidence stays fixed. Keywords: knowledge graphs; source attribution; classification; claim extraction; comparative concepts; Sinitic dialectology; Yue
item.dc:creator: Ksenia Kozha (American University of Cyprus), PaRAGraph Research Project

item.title: Learning Checklists to Reduce Lottery Effects in Scientific Peer Review
item.description: arXiv:2610.28666v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Reviewer lottery error describes error due to a small set of peer reviews attending to only some of the issues with a paper that a larger pool of eligible reviewers would raise. We show this error can be reduced by surfacing a checklist of criticisms learned from a historical review corpus. Our approach generates a tree of checklists representing coarsenings of the atomic review claim space, then selects the coarsening that maximizes a theoretically-motivated measure of correlated agreement among reviewers. We realize this approach with an LLM-assisted pipeline and test it on NeurIPS 2021 and ICLR 2022 review data. In simulated review with LLM reviewers, the learned checklist reduces the mean squared error (MSE) of a three reviewer committee by 58% on NeurIPS and 21% on ICLR, and on both venues the checklist with the highest correlated agreement has the lowest error for committees of three or more. In a human study with 20 participants, the learned NeurIPS checklist lowers the MSE of a paper ranking, measured against the NeurIPS 2021 order, from 0.48 to 0.22.
item.dc:creator: Xuanyou Liu, Ziyang Guo, Jason Hartline, Jessica Hullman

item.title: Epistemic Substitution: How Grokipedia's AI-Generated Encyclopedia Restructures Authority
item.description: arXiv:2512.03337v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: For more than two decades, Wikipedia has represented a decentralized, human-curated model of encyclopedic knowledge production. The emergence of AI-generated encyclopedias, such as Grokipedia, raises a fundamental question: do human- and AI-curated knowledge systems rely on the same foundations of epistemic authority? We examine this question through a comparative analysis of 1,000 matched Wikipedia--Grokipedia article pairs, comprising nearly 600,000 citation instances. Using an eight-category classification scheme, we construct the epistemic profiles of articles to examine the institutional composition of their cited sources. Our findings reveal substantial differences in sourcing practices. Grokipedia relies proportionally less on academic and journalistic sources and more on user-generated content and NGO and think-tank publications. These differences persist across broad topic domains, although their magnitude varies by subject. We also find that Grokipedia adds citations approximately linearly as articles grow, whereas Wikipedia exhibits greater variation in citation density. Together, these findings suggest a shift in the institutional sources invoked to justify encyclopedic claims, which we characterize as epistemic substitution. For the same topics, the two encyclopedias rest on different institutional sources. Our findings underscore the importance of systematic, ongoing audits of information provenance for accountability in generative knowledge systems.
item.dc:creator: Aliakbar Mehdizadeh, Faezeh Khazaee, Martin Hilbert
